title: How do you sanity check a strategy an AI wrote for you?
author: AoideusWasBanned
selftext:
I see a lot of people here asking ChatGPT or Claude for a strategy, getting a clean explanation plus some code, and going straight to a backtest. I use LLMs for parts of my own stuff too, and what I keep running into is that the explanation sounds great even when the code quietly does something wrong (like using the current candle's close before it's finished).

  
So I'm curious how you handle it:

  
\- Do you read every line of the code, or just look at the results?

\- What's the first thing you check when the backtest looks too good?

\- Do you ask the model to find its own bugs, and does that actually work?

  
Not after a perfect process, just wanna see how others do it. Thanks in advance.

comments.author: k1_r1
comments.body:
first check for me on any backtest that looks too good is shifting every signal one bar later. if the results fall apart, something was peeking at data it wouldnt have had yet, like the unfinished candle thing you mentioned. a real edge usually survives a one bar delay with some damage

i do read every line that touches entries, exits and position size. the explanation is the model telling you what it meant to write and the code is what it actually wrote, and those drift apart more than people think

asking it to find its own bugs works ok if the question is specific, like "list every place this uses data from the current bar." asking "is this right" just gets you a yes

i work on portfoliolab, which does the plain english rules to code to backtest loop, and the one bar delay is still the first thing i run on anything that looks too clean

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body: The one-bar delay test is a good one, cheap to run and it catches the sneaky stuff fast. If the edge falls apart after shifting signals by one bar, that's pretty much the answer.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the check that catches the most for me is truncating the data. run the signals on bars up to a date, then again with a month more added, and the old signals must not change. if new bars rewrite yesterday's signal, something reads ahead. the one bar shift catches the unfinished candle, this catches the scaled-over-the-whole-series kind. that check is the first thing I put into Quantradin when I built it. quantradin.com. what made you start asking?

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body: Mostly my own bugs tbh. I had a backtest that looked really good until I saw it was using the close of a candle that wasn't finished yet, and the code that did it read totally fine. The truncation test is a nice one, adding that to my list.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the unfinished candle one is the worst because the code looks right. same family as using the day's high to decide an entry you'd have made at 10am. the only thing that ever caught mine was running it live on paper next to the backtest and watching where they split.

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body: Same here, my paper bot fills didn't match the backtest at first. Did yours split mostly on fills or on the signals themselves?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: fills, mostly. once the look-ahead was out the signals matched almost bar for bar. the gap was options: the backtest filled at the mid, paper filled at the ask going in and the bid going out, and on a short hold that spread ate most of the edge.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: When a backtest looks too good, I'd first check for lookahead, like using a candle's close before the candle is finished. A quick test is to shift every signal by one bar. If the results collapse, the strategy was peeking. Running the same code on random or shuffled prices should also show no edge, and if it still makes money, something is wrong. Asking the model to review its own code can find some bugs, but it's no substitute for those tests, since it can miss the same mistake twice. Cymetica's Backtest Labs includes fees and holds out the last part of the history, which covers the out-of-sample part of the check.

comments.author: AnybodyIll6723
comments.body: The unfinished-candle thing you mentioned is a good example of why a clean explanation is a weak check: the model describes the strategy it meant to write, not the one in the code. One extra check that sits in front of the backtest is to write the entry and exit rules in plain language first, have the model implement only those, and reject any result you can't match trade-by-trade to that written list. Do you usually start with your own rules, or ask it to invent the strategy?

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body: Mostly my own rules first. I can trace each condition back to what I meant to test. If I ask an LLM for variants, I treat each one as a new hypothesis and check the logic and data window before trusting the result.

replies.author: AnybodyIll6723
replies.body: That's a solid split — starting from your own rules means you can actually trace each condition, and treating LLM variants as new hypotheses instead of free upgrades keeps the original test honest. The data-window check is the one I'd be strictest about, so a variant can't quietly borrow bars you already used to shape the first idea. When a variant fails that check, do you usually throw the whole thing out, or just shrink the window and try again?

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body: Mostly throw it out. If I shrink the window until it passes, I'm just fitting again with extra steps. I'd rather park the idea and test it later on data it hasn't seen.
